Design and analyses of renewables is based on special purpose computer tools with capability for integration of renewable energy resources and/or conversion technologies for multiple energy systems/sectors including energy demand and supply modelling. *It is a prerequisite for this module that students have their own laptop that operate the windows operating system. This is necessary to be able to install and operate the Homer Pro software necessary for practicals

title: Innovative Food Processes & Technology
description: The aim of this module is to provide a comprehensive understanding of new and emerging technologies and the rationale for adopting them in sustainable food processing. This module is designed for learners to become critically aware of the principles and applications of innovative and emerging food and bio-resource processing, and technologies that meet the demands for sustainable and safe food systems. A series of lectures, tutorials, practical and virtual laboratories, webinars and seminars will inform learners of both thermal and non thermal technologies. Specific case studies will be used to illustrate potential applications, regulatory aspects and the role of emerging technologies and processing in the circular bio-economy. Indicative Syllabus: The rationale and drivers of novel process technologies. Principles of key novel processing technologies, their preservation mechanisms, effects on food quality characteristics as well as the effects on structural and physicochemical properties inherent to each innovative approach will be emphasised. Principle areas of focus will be on Innovations in both Thermal and Non-thermal processing technologies promoting sustainable food systems at different stages along the food chain. Technologies include Mild Heat processing, Microwave, High pressure processing, Infra Red, Pulsed Electric Field, Light such as UV, LED and photo-sensitisation approaches as well as advanced oxidative technologies such as Cold Plasma, Ozone, Ultrasound. Enzymatic processes as well as Continuous separation technologies and green chemical interventions. Emerging food engineering processes of importance for the circular bioeconomy include the integration of microalgae technology as a waste valorization and co-product development strategy as well as microencapsulation, extrusion and 3dprinting with a focus on alternative proteins. Process technologies can allow all 4S aspects to be achieved with food or food waste streams. Integration with existing processes, advantages and limitations by comparison with traditional technologies will promote critical evaluation and reflection on selection and adoption of appropriate process design.

title: Deliver agrifood business plan
description: Pass/Fail (GPA Neutral) This module will bring the activities of the programme to the DELIVER stage. Each team will focus on refining their ideas, consolidating the case for their proposition, validating the feasibility, preparing pitches for R&D support and business support, and finishing with the submission of a funding request (whether for comm funding or business funding)(subject to quality control by the module coordinator).

title: Agrifood: need to investment
description: Pass/Fail (GPA Neutral) This module will prepare each individual, and the team they are part of, to be able to DEVELOP the solution for the need they have identified. The module will take some of the theoretical ideas introduced earlier in the programme and put them into practice in the context of the specific Need-User-Solution-Customer context. It will address topics including prototype development; IP protection and licensing; creating a functioning business team; and funding.

title: Agrifood solutions
description: Pass/Fail (GPA Neutral) This module will prepare each individual, and the team they are part of, to be able to DEVELOP the solution for the need they have identified. The module will provide the skills needed to identify the stakeholders involved in the sale of the solution, including users, recommenders, buyers and influences. This will form the basis of customer discovery, segmentation and validation. Market tools will be used to estimate the size of the market, the accessible proportion and the likely penetration. These will form the basis for creating a first draft business plan and financial forecast for the proposed solution.

title: Develop: agrifood innovation
description: Pass/Fail (GPA Neutral) This module will help participants DEVELOP solutions for the needs identified in the DISCOVER stage of the programme. There will be three distinct activities: (1) Exposure to technology ideas - planned engagement with RPO researchers to find possible technical solutions and understand the best R&D environment for new ideas to be advanced (2) Self-directed engagement with technology solution providers (anywhere in the world). (3) A cycle of proposing, evaluating, testing, rejecting/accepting until the best possible solution is identified By the end of the module, each team will have a clearly defined solution developed that addresses one or more specific user needs. This will be defined in terms of: (a) user; (b) need(s); (c) solution; (d) features; (e) R&D requirements to implement; (f) preliminary DESIGN

title: Agrifood business development
description: Pass/Fail (GPA Neutral) This module prepares the participants to bring their ideas beyond the 3D stage of the programme, towards R&D innovation funding and the establishment of a business. It covers the fundamentals of laboratory-to-market entrepreneurship including matching needs to technologies, business models, the systematic innovation cycle, market fit, intellectual property, funding a business and funding specific R&D activities.

title: Agrifood needs-led innovation
description: Pass/Fail (GPA Neutral) This module is delivers the principles and methods to support the DISCOVERY activity for the programme. It also includes health and safety and check-ins with coaches/mentors each week. It outlines the 3D method: Discover, Develop and Deliver, and then focuses on how to get the most from observation and interview during an immersive situation in a working environment. It then examines the team building process to help participants understand their role, and the role of other team members in the formation of an effective innovation team.

title: Discover: Agrifood Immersion
description: Pass/Fail (GPA Neutral) This module delivers the main DISCOVERY activity for the programme. The module will provide the programme participants with immersion into the agri-food system, focusing on the farm, supplier, logistics and processing business environments. Each aspect of the supply chain will be introduced by an expert (e.g., researcher, advisor, business leader) prior to site visits. The participants will spend 3 days per site observing activities, asking questions and understanding what is happening. They will follow this up by self-directed engagement with a wider group of actors to help identify and validate (ie., DISCOVER) needs.

title: Capstone Research Project
description: This module allows final-year students to apply their course knowledge to a real-world problem through a design, experimental, or systems analysis project. Students must plan with a supervisor, conduct a literature review, assess possible solutions, and apply scientific and engineering principles. Weekly meetings with the coordinator support progress. The final submission includes a written report (with literature review, design drawings, health and safety considerations for your research, and data collation and analysis) and an oral presentation. The project should demonstrate understanding of key concepts, ethical and safety issues, and problem-solving abilities.

title: UCD-NE DD Credit Recognition
description: Pass/Fail (GPA Neutral) Credit transfer module for 60 ECTS completed at NU.

title: AI applications in Eng&Sci
description: This module introduces the principles and applications of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), generative AI, and scientific large language models in scientific and engineering domains, with particular emphasis on agri-food, health, life science, and biosystems applications. It aims to equip students with the conceptual understanding, practical computational skills, and critical judgement required to apply data-driven approaches to real-world scientific and engineering problems. The module adopts an interdisciplinary, application-oriented, and learning-by-doing approach. It is designed to be accessible to students with limited prior programming experience, while supporting progression towards independent and critical use of AI methods. Through hands-on activities using Python-based environments such as Google Colab and VS Code, students will develop practical experience in data processing, visualisation, feature engineering, model development, validation, evaluation, and interpretation. In addition to traditional machine learning and deep learning methods, the module introduces the role of generative AI and scientific large language models in coding support, data analysis, knowledge extraction, and scientific problem-solving. Students will be encouraged to critically evaluate AI outputs with regard to reliability, uncertainty, bias, reproducibility, domain relevance, and responsible use. The module is contextualised through case studies from agri-food, health, life science, and engineering applications. Examples may include bioactive compound discovery, precision fermentation, food quality and safety assessment, formulation and flavour design, sensory and consumer data analysis, nutrition modelling, and biomedical or biochemical data analysis. A central component of the module is a project-based learning experience in which students design and implement an AI-driven solution to a scientific or engineering problem relevant to their academic or research interests. Through this project, students will integrate computational methods with domain knowledge, justify methodological choices, interpret results critically, and communicate technical findings effectively.

title: LCA & Green Technologies
description: *** Not available in the academic year indicated above *** This award provides industry-aligned training in environmental assessment, sustainable energy systems, and emerging green technologies, equipping participants with the practical skills needed to support the transition to a low-carbon, resource-efficient economy across sectors including agri-food, energy, manufacturing, and environmental consultancy. The programme integrates three key components: Life Cycle Assessment (LCA), Sustainable Energy Systems and Environmental Impact, and a Green Technologies Project. Learners develop a strong foundation in internationally recognised LCA methodologies, gain the ability to evaluate energy systems using techno-economic and environmental criteria, and apply critical thinking and research skills to assess the sustainability of emerging green technologies. Developed in response to industry demand and informed by engagement with enterprise partners, the programme addresses growing workforce needs driven by the EU Green Deal, Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), and corporate net-zero commitments. Graduates will acquire transferable skills in data analysis, systems thinking, environmental modelling, and sustainability reporting, enhancing their career opportunities and supporting Ireland’s green and digital transition.

title: Sust Assessment & Reporting
description: *** Not available in the academic year indicated above *** The Professional Diploma in Sustainability Assessment and Reporting is an interdisciplinary Level 9 programme designed to equip learners with the knowledge and practical skills required to address contemporary sustainability challenges across industry, business, engineering, and the public sector. The programme provides a comprehensive understanding of sustainability assessment methodologies, carbon footprinting, greenhouse gas accounting, ESG reporting, systems thinking, circular economy principles, life-cycle thinking, and sustainability-oriented innovation. Through a combination of challenge-based learning, case studies, project-based activities, and applied sustainability assessment tools, learners develop the ability to evaluate environmental, economic, and social sustainability performance and design evidence-based sustainability solutions. The programme emphasises practical implementation, critical thinking, interdisciplinary collaboration, and professional communication, preparing graduates to support organisations in responding to emerging sustainability, climate, and regulatory requirements while contributing to the transition towards a low-carbon, circular, and resilient economy.

title: Museums and Collections
description: This Stage 1 core module is only for students on the Classics, Art History and Archaeology BA Humanities programme. It provides an introduction to the historical, social, and theoretical contexts of museums and collections, as well as to the interpretive methodologies applied to some of the main categories of artefacts from prehistory to the modern world. Ceramics, inscriptions, paintings and photographs are some of the materials covered, with seminars also looking at issues such as conservation, digital cultural heritage and curation. The cultural heritage collections of UCD are embedded in this module, with classes taking place in the Classical Museum, the Centre for Experimental Archaeology and Material Culture and with the Kingsley Photographic Collection, as well as a visit to the National Gallery of Ireland. This module also provides training in key skills for a BA Humanities degree in UCD.

title: Digital Pasts: Technology and Cultural Heritage
description: Digital Pasts: Technology and Cultural Heritage is a core module for Stage 2 students on the Classics, Art History and Archaeology BA Humanities programme (there are no Elective/Study Abroad places available). The module focuses on how digital technologies are transforming the ways we engage with, preserve, and understand the past. As digital tools become increasingly central to cultural heritage work, from documentation and analysis to public interpretation and global accessibility, this module offers both practical training and critical reflection on these changes. Students will gain hands-on experience with tools used to digitise, preserve, interpret, and share cultural heritage. Classes will focus on topics such as photogrammetry and 3D scanning, augmented/enhanced reality, GIS, machine learning and AI, LiDAR and Remote Sensing, museums and technology, databases, and digital storytelling. Alongside this, students will engage critically with the theoretical, ethical, environmental, and political dimensions of digital heritage, including digital repatriation, representation, and sustainability. The module draws on cutting-edge, digitally driven research within the Schools of Classics, Art History, and Archaeology, and includes contributions from staff working on a range of innovative cultural heritage projects.

title: Dissertation
description: This module provides a unique and exciting opportunity to carry out a piece of substantial research that builds on the knowledge, skills and methods developed over the course of the Classics, Art History and Archaeology programme. It is only for students on this degree pathway or other BA Humanities degrees as approved by programme directors. Students will work with an assigned academic supervisor to produce an independently researched dissertation. Following successful completion of a research skills module in the preceding Autumn trimester (GRC30580 Dissertation Preparation), students will use primary and secondary sources to develop their project, leading to a clearly argued and organised piece of writing of c.8000 words, with an accompanying bibliography; the dissertation also may include illustrations, plans, tables and appendices as appropriate.

title: Cultural Policy in Context
description: Working in the creative and cultural industries requires an understanding of cultural policy. Through reading, discussion, and creative activities, students will build understanding of how cultural policy relates to creative and cultural ecosystems and practices, including their own. With universities a part of the creative and cultural ecosystem of Dublin and Ireland (and internationally), UCD will serve as a bounded case study through which students will synthesise their learning about cultural policy. By engaging directly with policy documents and processes, students will apply their learning to the development of a university-wide policy aimed at supporting the creative and cultural life of UCD students.

title: Meet the Makers
description: Meet the Makers is a platform for students to engage with artists, designers, cultural entrepreneurs and producers working throughout the creative and cultural industries. Each week we will meet with practitioners and professionals from the wider field of arts and culture to discuss different facets of creative work, artistic development, media engagement, career paths, and navigation through the contemporary creative and cultural industries. Individual site visits to cultural venues and events will also form part of the module. This module is co-coordinated by Prof. Emily Mark-Fitzgerald (Head of Subject, CCI), and Dafe Pessu Orugbo (award-winning multi-disciplinary artist).

title: Video Games: History, Technology, and Culture
description: This module is being taught in 2026-7 by Dr Michael Iantorno (https://michaeliantorno.com/) This module will provide an introduction to the origins and transformations of the videogame industry from the 1970s to the modern day. It will discuss how games are created by stakeholders ranging from independent artists to massive media corporations; interrogate their history as consumer hardware, software, and platforms; and consider the discourses that construct and challenge heteronormative and exclusionary gamer identities. This module will provide students with foundational knowledge about what games are, who makes them, and how they intersect with legacy media industries such as music, film, and journalism. In addition to written assignments, students will have the opportunity to become game developers themselves by engaging with open-source software such as Twine, GB Studio, and Bitsy and publishing on free platforms such as itch.io.

title: Introduction to Creative & Cultural Industries
description: This module serves as an introduction to the interdisciplinary study of Creative & Cultural industries, providing an initial exploration of the world of creative and cultural production and setting the stage for subsequent modules in the CCI program. The module surveys the industrial ecosystem of creative and cultural work, introducing students to creative vocations, organisations, and policies. Built upon an interdisciplinary literature drawn from cultural studies, political economy, sociology, and organisation studies, the module is intended to give students the necessary analytical tools to critically assess and prepare for their future careers as creative and cultural workers. It will introduce the key themes, thinkers, and debates that students will engage as they make their way through the Creative & Cultural Industries program. *Note: this module is being taught in 2026-27 by Dr Benjamin Anderson.

title: Introduction to Digital Media
description: In 2026-7, this module is being taught by Dr Michael Iantorno (https://michaeliantorno.com/) Introduction to Digital Media offers an introduction to the rapidly evolving world of digital media. Combining theory and practice, students will thoughtfully engage in the study of digital culture, media policy, industry labour, and more. By developing their own digital media projects and critically analysing cultural production, this module will help students cultivate their creative practices and learn what it means to be part of an increasingly technologised world. The three core subject areas for this module are: audio production, video production, and artificial intelligence (AI) literacy. Students will be taught how to use Reaper/Audacity for audio editing and DaVinci Resolve for video editing.

title: Managing Culture
description: The creative and cultural industries are 'people businesses' but what does this actually mean in practice? This module will give you theoretical and practical skills to build your portfolio of understanding whether you plan to work for yourself, start your own business or enter an existing organisation.

title: Introduction to Art Law
description: This module will be taught by Martin Bradley, Barrister-at-Law, and specialist in art and cultural heritage law. This module will introduce the legal and regulatory frameworks that apply to art, culture and heritage by examining Irish and international laws, regulations and conventions that govern these fields. Consideration of moral and ethical principles will also be included. Definitions of art, heritage and culture in law will be examined, along with key issues such as copyright, intellectual property, imports and exports, restitution and repatriation, decolonisation, Nazi-era spoliation, national monuments, listed buildings and their contents, underwater cultural heritage, art crime, fraud and theft, tax, title and provenance.

title: Labour and Film
description: *Note: this is a new module offered by a new member of Creative & Cultural Industries staff, Dr. Benjamin Anderson, a specialist on labour and media. Students from CCI, Film Studies, and electives are welcome to enrol.* Labour and film share a common history, both in terms of film production and cinematic representation. This module investigates this mutual history through the examination of popular cultural depictions of the labour movement and the working class. At the same time, it explores the nature of work in the film industry and the ways in which this work contributes to the production and dissemination of narratives of work and class. It does so by connecting critical literature in film and media studies with core texts in labour studies, political economy, and working-class history. This literature is further supplemented with a weekly screening of a film illustrating the thematic exploration for each unit of the module.

title: Minding Your Business
description: In 2026-7 this module will be taught by our new CCI colleague, Dr Michael Iantorno (https://michaeliantorno.com/). Module content and assessment details will be updated in due course. Minding Your Business is a practical skills module designed to prepare students for post-graduate working life. The goal of this module isn’t to teach you how to work in your chosen field but rather to how to find work, how to sustain it and how to value it. Through a blend of lectures that contextualise the contemporary creative & cultural landscape and professional practice, students will not only generate the materials needed to enter the workforce successfully but also develop the ability to communicate their skillset effectively.

title: Research as Creative Thinking
description: In CCI30030 Research as Creative Thinking, students will be introduced to key approaches to research in the arts, humanities and social sciences with the goal of using these to develop their capstone projects. Through lectures, guest presentations, readings, activities and assessments, students will be challenged to reflect on and develop techniques for developing research ideas and articulating research problems, formulating research plans, collecting and analysing data, and writing research reports. Students will be introduced to the research process, key methodological orientations and theoretical streams in Creative & Cultural Industries, and specific approaches including documentary and archival research, ethnography and action research, discourse and rhetorical analysis, and creative practice based approaches.

title: Capstone Project
description: This module is worth 15 credits and is required for the BA in Creative and Cultural Industries programme. It is the culminating individual capstone project for CCI students, demonstrating their capacity to initiate and realise a major creative and research project, showcasing their knowledge, skills, and abilities. It is an opportunity to take ownership of learning, and hone creative voice and ambitions. Final projects will demonstrate a refined understanding of the context of the creative and cultural industries; will anticipate audiences for the work; and critically reflect on their own emerging role as a creative professional in relation to the political, economic, social, cultural, artistic and technological trends and factors that influence the field as a whole. The final form of capstone projects will be diverse, and may take the form of written work, events, digital projects, film/screen-based projects, etc. The final project is also an opportunity to demonstrate to future employers or collaborators the student's skills and abilities. Selecting from one of three strands -- research dissertation; creative project based on UCD Collections; or creative project (open) -- students will be assigned an individual supervisor, and work to develop their project proposals developed in the autumn trimester (as part of CCI30030 - Research as Creative Thinking). All projects will involve some element of critical writing, appropriate in proportion to the proposed final deliverable project. The majority of student hours will be spent engaged in individual research and development. Student work will be presented during a final series of group sessions that will include external industry participation; and as a final completed project.

title: Sustainability and Culture
description: How do the creative and cultural industries respond to and grapple with injunctions to ‘go green’, ‘be sustainable,’ and/or to respond to climate change? How do broader factors, like inequality, worker precarity, consumption, and/ or globalization impact on efforts by creative workers and industries to respond to urgent environmental challenges? How might creative works themselves posit alternate imaginaries or ways of engaging with the world more sustainability (to live more slowly, divest from fossil fuels, or promote collectivity and/or solidarity)? In this module, students will gain a greater understanding of sustainability discourse and its relationship to creative and cultural industry policy and practice across a range of related areas, ranging from making creative work, production and management in sectors such as the performing and visual arts, galleries/ museums, publishing, and creative writing. In bringing together different disciplinary perspectives, it will equip students with knowledge of some of the key debates taking place regarding sustainability and culture, with attention paid to the intersecting impact of environmental, economic, political, and social forces. We will bring in local and international case studies, along with guest practitioners, to assist in making sense of how these issues unfold and are addressed. Topics which may be considered include sustainability, climate action and cultural policy – from the UN to Ireland; big publishing and slow writing; small publishing and sustainability in Ireland; arts award culture and greenwashing; greening artforms and events; sustainable prosperity and creative work. This interdisciplinary module will be relevant to any student interested in creative practice and how they intersect with the key environmental challenges of our time. No previous expertise in creative and cultural industries or policy is assumed or necessary. This module is co-designed and convened by Dr Treasa De Loughry (English, Drama and Film) and Dr Victoria Durrer (Art History and Cultural Policy) and is designed for students across English Litertature and Creative Writing, and Creative and Cultural Industries.

title: Work & Labour in Creative, Cultural and Media Industries
description: CCI30070 Work & Labour in Creative, Cultural and Media Industries introduces students to key issues faced by creative, cultural and media workers. Set against an interdisciplinary reading list drawn from sociology of work, critical political economy, labour geography, cultural economy and beyond, the module extends students previous studies in CCI by challenging them to critically examine the roles, responsibilities, and conditions of work in the cultural sector broadly defined. They will be challenged to think through challenges including precarious employment, gendered and racialised inequalities, overwork, and exploitation, as well as possible alternatives and correctives to these, particularly in the form of worker organising and collective action.

title: Introduction to Celtic Civilization
description: This introductory module provides students with an overview of the history, languages, archaeological remains and literature of the Celtic-speaking peoples from prehistoric to medieval times. The main focus is on the question of 'who are the Celts'. It forms a solid foundation from which students can progress to study the legacy of the Celts in greater detail at stages 2 and 3. In the face of so many confusing modern claims about 'the Celts', the module adopts a fact-based approach, starting with the descriptions of the peoples called Keltoi/Celti by Classical Greek and Roman authors. Starting with this solid basis, we move fast forward to the end of the 17th century when European scholars once again cast their eyes on the ancient Celts and speculated their relationship with the contemporary peoples and languages. We will then introduce the scientific method of historical linguistics, and use it to reconstruct the modern linguistic conception of the Celtic languages. The history and form of major groups of ancient and modern Celtic languages, such as Gaulish, Celtiberian, Brythonic and Goidelic languages, will be presented in term, with a special lecture on the mystic Pictish language. We will use one lecture also to discuss the importance of onomastics in the study of the history of the Celts and other peoples in Europe. We will then plunge into the fascinating world of archaeological and art remains of the peoples that we can now more confidently called 'the Celts' based on the first part of the course. We will talk about the 'Celticisation' of Ireland, with special attention paid to the enigmatic prehistory of Ireland, followed by a summary lecture on how language, artifact and DNA can be used together to reveal the past. After the Halloween break (Week 8), we turn to the Christianisation of Ireland, and the topic of Druids and pre-Christian belief in Ireland. Then we will talk about the role of the king in Ireland, the literary traditions of the insular Celtic peoples, some major native works regarding the prehistory of Ireland and Wales. The last week of the term will be dedicated to the decline of the Celtic languages and the modern imaginations of the Celts. It is hoped that after studying this module, students will be able to tell how the concept of 'Celtic' came into existence, what evidence is in support of the theories, what happened to the various Celtic-speaking peoples, and how to evaluate the different claims about the 'Celts' in modern society. All texts will be read in translation, supported by critical reading, and no previous knowledge of a Celtic language is required. Beginners’ modules in medieval Irish and Welsh (CCIV30070 & CCIV20100) are also available for those wishing to study the languages of the primary sources.

title: Early Ireland: Continuity & Change
description: Students will need a laptop and Wifi connection to participate fully in this module. *Traffic Light Red: Students are not permitted to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) in this module.* The course is designed as an introduction to early Irish society and culture. The period we cover was one of great change for Irish society – the arrival of Christianity with a new language, the rise of new, forceful power groupings and the opportunities and challenges posed by the intrusion of the Vikings. Underlying these transformations there was continuity and we will examine the evidence for the survival of earlier belief – in the burial record and in the role of women in the administration of associated rituals. We will look at the institution of kingship, with its rituals & taboos grounded in Paganism. Changes in the manifestation of kingship, especially the growth of over-kingship were a feature of this period. St Patrick, symbolic of Irish Christianity, was brought to Ireland as a slave and as the Vikings arrive the slave trade becomes more visible. We will consider the position of slaves in Irish society – their role in the running of the household and in the labour–intensive agricultural economy. This was one of the most dynamic periods in Irish history. A glance at the beautiful high crosses scattered across the Irish landscape indicate the wealth, patronage of the arts and appreciation of innovative ideas that were a mark of this era.

title: The British Celts
description: The module gives an overview of the early history of the Celtic-speaking peoples in Britain. After outlining what we know of Late Iron Age Britain, we study the wide-ranging changes caused by Roman Conquest, and examine what can be learned from various types of evidence about aspects of daily life, art and religion. When the Romans left we consider what was their enduring legacy, and what the newly independent Britain was once again like before the arrival of a new external threat with the coming of Germanic speakers, the ancestors of the English. These are the 'Dark Ages' in terms of scanty direct textual documentations, when traditions associated with the enigmatic but influential figure of Arthur developed. We also examine the emergence of new kingdoms and see how Christianity spread over the whole land. Finally we look at the languages and written culture of late antique and early meideval Britain, starting with the earliest evidence of the British Celtic languages such as curse tablets and burial stones, but focusing on medieval Welsh literature, such as the heroic poems and the magical Mabinogion narratives, which are read in translation.

title: Vikings in the Celtic World
description: Students will need a laptop and Wifi connection to participate fully in this module. *Traffic Light Red: Students are not permitted to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) in this module.* This course will consider the Viking experience of the Celtic-speaking lands and how the Vikings, through both confrontation and collaboration, had a transformative impact on that world between c. 780 – 1020. The Vikings were largely a silent people and it is largely through the eyes of those they encountered – peoples who were already literate – that we first get to know them. Many of our enduring images of the Vikings are based on sources from the Celtic world, and some of the earliest and most complete accounts of the initial Viking raids are found in the Irish annals. As the Vikings become a permanent presence in these lands, the Celtic and Norse views of the spiritual, heroic and economic world intersected and, at times, collided. We will look at the manner in which the Vikings are treated in literature and how this changes over time. We will trace the survival of rituals and beliefs brought from Scandinavia as exemplified by the decorated slabs and burials on the Isle of Man, where legends from Norse mythology feature on Christian crosses and a warrior was buried with a sacrificed slave. There were personalities, both Norse and Celtic, who straddled both worlds, and many of these men and women were nurtured in both traditions and reflect the enduring and transforming contacts made through intermarriage, fosterage and political alliances. The emergence of new dynasties and kingdoms is a product of the special circumstances of this period and we will consider how they arise and what their impact was on the wider Norse and Celtic worlds. Towns develop in the west and the north as a result of the Vikings’ new raiding/trading activities, and the connections between the contemporary developments of Dublin, Waterford and Limerick in Ireland and Kaupang, Birka and Hedeby in Scandinavia will be surveyed. This multifaceted course will provide students with a clear understanding of this fascinating and dynamic period in the history of the Norse and Celtic worlds.

title: Poets, Power and Performance
description: *Traffic Light Red: Students are not permitted to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) in this module.* This module draws on the languages and literatures of the Celtic languages to explore the role of the poet and the power of words, extending back to the earliest written evidence. The first half of the module examines the organisation of the professional poets and their status in medieval Irish society (c. 600-1200), focusing on their primary functions of praise and satire. Literary sources, such as saga material and our earliest known praise poem, will be analysed to illustrate the social significance of praise poetry and the integral role played by the poet in medieval Irish society. Drawing on a corpus of legal and poetical material, we will also study the language of satire and in its many forms, from mockery, ridicule and name-calling to invectives and curses. In the second half of the module, we examine the power of words as magical agents in verse and song, including the lament. The efficacy of the spoken and written word in prayers, charms and curses will also be analysed. The vital role of these phenomena will be placed in a framework of traditional life in Ireland and discussed in relation to vernacular life. The social status and role of the poet as found in Irish oral tradition will also be highlighted. We will learn how to scan a medieval Irish poem, and trace the development of Irish metrics and styles through the centuries. We will examine the functions of poetry in its society, such as spells, curses, grammatical examples, law texts and historiography. The performance of poetry in various social settings tells us much about the lives of poets and the perception of the power of words. We will also discuss poetry as an arcane art that empowers subversion of time-space, hierarchy and gender roles in the forms of prophecy, keening and poetic duels, in which women play an important part.

title: Intro to Medieval Welsh
description: Welsh is the oldest living language of Britain, and is related closely to Cornish and Breton (together forming the Brythonic or British branch of the Celtic languages), and more distantly to Irish and the other languages of the Goidelic branch of Celtic. Written texts in Welsh survive from around the eighth century, and from the mid-thirteenth century onward we have a large number of manuscripts in Welsh containing a rich assortment of material, including such highlights as the love and nature poetry of Dafydd ap Gwilym and the enchanting tales of the Mabinogion. This module offers beginners in the language a carefully-graded introduction to this rich field.

title: Law & Society in Early Ireland
description: Early Irish law ('Brehon law') was first recorded in the 7th century CE and survived as a living tradition until the 17th century. It has the earliest and most copious textual tradition written in a vernacular language (i.e. not Latin or Greek) in Europe. The surviving law texts provide a highly valuable window to observe the culture, society and even bee-keeping and divorce arrangement in medieval Ireland. Students will not only learn of this rich and interesting legal tradition, but also understand the details of a society very different from ours. This module is an excellent complement to majors in Celtic Civilisation, Irish, History and Law. The first part of the module examines the sources from which we know about early Irish law, including manuscripts, major compilations of law, layers of texts and families of legal scholars in late medieval Ireland. The second part deals with the contents of early Irish law. We will cover the main categories such as law of persons, law of property, injury and compensation, legal procedures, etc. While explaining the legal institutions we will observe how they reflect social practices such as contracts, neighbourhood, farming techniques and gender relationship. The third and final part focusses on the interaction between law, literature and politics. We will question whether one can firmly distinguish between law and literature, and trace how law was used to promote political claims and cultural identity. Students will be assessed by a short in-class test and two essays during the module.

title: Kings and Heroes of Early Ireland
description: Students will need a laptop and Wifi connection to participate fully in this module. *Traffic Light Red: Students are not permitted to use generative artificial intelligence (AI) in this module.* The Ulster Cycle tales are among the best-known narratives of Early Irish literature (c. 700-1200 AD). The tales depict the heroic society of pagan Ireland and the rivalry for supremacy between Ulster and Connacht. We will study, in translation, not just the centre-piece of the cycle (The 'Táin' or 'Cattle Raid of Cooley'), but also other major and minor tales, which offer an introduction to the wide variety of themes, genres, and literary styles of one branch of this uniquely early literature. Among the most attractive and accessible of the Early Irish tales are those dealing with the lives of legendary or early historical kings and heroes, such as Cormac mac Airt, about whom many tales have survived. We will read these sagas in translation, to discover how legendary and historical kings are presented as admirable or otherwise, what the desirable characteristics of an ideal king were, and how the demands of kingship were reconciled with the king's human needs. More generally we consider what were the pressing concerns of the social and political ruling elites of Early Ireland, and how how they were encoded and explored in a memorable literature.

title: Introduction to Early Irish 1
description: This module will introduce students to basic aspects of Early Irish grammar, phonology, orthography and syntax. Students will develop a basic vocabulary including nouns, verbs and prepositions through the completion of graded exercises. Previous experience of learning languages would be an advantage.

title: Intro to Medieval Welsh 2
description: This module continues from CCIV 20100 and aims to finish Part 1 (grammar) of Miles' textbook. If there is time left, we will continue into Part 2 and read Middle Welsh sagas and poems withe the help of dictionaries.

title: Introduction to Early Irish 2
description: This Course builds on CCIV20110, and uses the same method to extend the student's command of vocabulary, word-forms and sentence-structure. Each unit deals with new vocabulary and a new grammatical concept, which are practised by means of translation of increasingly complex sentences.

title: Early Irish Myths & Sagas
description: Hundreds of myths and sagas survive from medieval Ireland. Many of these display intricate narrative techniques and structures, and their contents often reflect contemporary ideologies as well as inherited mythological motifs. In this module we will focus on one specific long narrative from the early Middle Ages and conduct a thorough and critical analysis of the text. No knowledge of Old Irish is required, as we will read the story in full in English translation, but throughout the module key Irish terms and concepts will be examined and their significance explained. The module provides a chance to closely read an early Irish narrative text and to analyse the author's ideologies and the techniques s/he used. It deepens the students' understanding of early Irish literature and culture. Topics covered in the module include: -- text version, recension and intertextuality -- narrative techniques -- ideologies of kingship, justice and gender -- genres and cycles Students are assessed by one short report and one final essay, as well as participation in online discussions and quizzes.

title: Descriptive Geometry and Engineering Drawing
description: Descriptive Geometry and Engineering Drawing is a technical basic course. It is a subject about the theories and methods of studying making and reading engineering drawings and solving spatial geometry problems by projection. At the same time, students’ ability to draw engineering graphics using computers is being developed. In the study, students are required to master projection theory and application, especially orthographic projection, learn graphic methods of spatial measuring and positioning problems, learn the method of making and reading engineering drawings, and learn to draw by using a computer.

description: This course is compulsory for the students who major in transportation. The basic concepts, theories, methods and application of transportation planning are systematically taught during this course. It focuses on the basic methods of transportation planning, the basic concepts and theories of traffic demand forecasting and the practical application of transportation planning.

title: Geom. Graphics & Mech. Drawing
description: This course is a technology basic lesson of mechanical majors. It is the subject that studies the graphic method and graphic method of solving space geometry problems on the plane. This course helps students lay a foundation for reading and drawing of mechanical drawings in advance.

description: Purpose & Overarching Content Advanced mathematics is one of the important basic theoretical courses for college students, who major in engineering. The course helps students to grasp: (1) Calculus of functions of one variable; (2) Basic conception of ordinary differential equation, basic theory and basic arithmetic skills, a necessary mathematical foundation to further study the successive courses and mathematical knowledge.

title: English 1
description: OVSE1003W English for University Studies is designed for students who have embarked on the first trimester of their dual undergraduate degree programme in Civil Engineering Infrastructure, Automotive Engineering, or Transport City Planning & Environmental Policy at Chang'an-Dublin International College. The module aims to help students develop their English language proficiency in the context of university study and prepare them for the tasks they will face while doing an English-medium higher education degree. The content is organised around themes which reflect key aspects of university life in the early stages. The core skills of listening, reading, speaking and writing are integrated and linked around each theme, and emphasis is placed on the functions and language required for different communicative purposes. More specifically, the listening component of the course focuses on the listening comprehension strategies students need when participating in group discussions and attending lectures and gives students practice in concurrent note-taking and listening. The reading tasks expose students to a variety of texts and introduce different reading purposes and strategies, note-taking and summarising and synthesizing information from different sources. The writing classes are designed to help students write definitions, purpose statements, short texts and responses to (exam) questions drawing upon information from a reading passage. Students will have the opportunity to develop their speaking skills by giving oral summaries and short presentations (on topics of social and general academic interest) and through participation in group discussions. The course also helps students to expand the range and improve the accuracy of lexis and grammatical structures they use in written and spoken texts. In addition to focusing on the above language-related skills, classroom tasks and activities support students’ development of academic study competences, independent language learning strategies and critical thinking skills. This module will be delivered via small group teaching with classes having a maximum of 20 students. Students are expected to work collaboratively as well as to engage in various independent study tasks throughout the course. They will be strongly encouraged to take responsibility for their own learning and use strategies for improving specific language skills independently. Materials and assessments for the module are designed with reference to upper-B1 and B2 descriptors of the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) and The British Association of Lecturers in English for Academic Purposes (BALEAP)’s ‘can-do’ framework for EAP syllabus design and assessment.

title: English 2
description: CDIC1028W - English 2 (English for General Academic Purposes) is designed for Stage 1 Students who are undertaking dual undergraduate degree programmes at Chang’an-Dublin International College. The module specifically aims to develop students' academic English and study skills, with a view to preparing them for independent study in English on their degree programmes. There is a focus throughout the semester on the UN's 17 Sustainable Development Goals. In this context, students develop their English vocabulary and grammar for general academic purposes. They learn useful collocations and idioms, how to use vocabulary precisely, and strategies for dealing with unfamiliar vocabulary. They become familiar with the grammar patterns they are most likely to encounter in academic and semi-academic texts, and work on overcoming common grammar errors. Classes integrate the key skills of Listening, Reading, Writing and Speaking. Students learn how to listen for key information in day-to-day conversations and to take notes from lectures on topics of general interest. They gain experience of listening to a range of accents and develop strategies for coping with fast or unclear speech. When reading, they learn how to skim for the main idea of a text, to scan for specific information, and to read closely in order to understand more complex ideas. Meanwhile, they develop their writing skills at the level of sentence, paragraph and whole text. There is an emphasis on how to structure their writing through the effective use of thesis statements and topic sentences supported by explanations and examples. They learn how to write factual, descriptive texts in response to visual data, and how to write a problem-solution essay. They learn how to write under time pressure and without relying upon translation software or other aids. In terms of speaking, students will work on fluency, pronunciation, and organizing what they say. They will gain experience of presenting their views on issues of general academic interest, and of interacting in seminar-style discussions of more abstract topics. All classes work towards a further aim of helping students to develop their critical thinking skills. Classes are taught in small groups of up to 20 students. In addition to developing language skills, classroom activities will support the development of students’ academic study competences and independent language learning strategies. Students will often be expected to work collaboratively in class. Materials and assessments for the module are designed with reference to B2 descriptors of the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) and The British Association of Lecturers in English for Academic Purposes (BALEAP)’s ‘can-do’ framework for EAP syllabus design and assessment.

title: English 3
description: OVSE2007W English 3 is designed for Stage 2 students who are undertaking a dual undergraduate degree programme at Chang’an University. The module aims to help students develop their general academic English language and particularly the skills of spoken production, spoken interaction and writing. The module encourages them to become effective independent learners. The content reflects themes which are common across academic disciplines (e.g. education, communication, technology, etc.) and students explore these from different perspectives (e.g. economic, technological, legal, social, business). Classroom tasks and activities allow students to replicate the processes they go through in their academic studies. More specifically, students develop their spoken interaction skills through active participation in seminar discussions and they improve their spoken production skills through short presentations. The academic writing classes are designed to take students through the different stages involved in the process of producing written academic assignments and help them develop their writing skills incrementally from sentences, to paragraph structure, to different types of essay (comparison, argumentative, cause and effect, problem-solution) and timed writing tasks. The receptive skills of listening and reading are also addressed, with an emphasis on effective note-taking, paraphrasing, and summarizing. Students learn how to integrate sources into their own writing. Students also have the opportunity to expand the range and improve the accuracy of academic language (vocabulary, grammar, lexical and grammatical patterns) they use in written and spoken texts. In addition to the above language-related skills, academic competence and critical thinking are integral parts of the course. Classroom activities support students’ development of: (a) academic study competences (e.g. conveying meaning successfully in speaking and writing, etc.), (b) independent language learning strategies (e.g. finding, analyzing and recording useful language, creating key word lists, etc.). Critical thinking is practised in relation to all aspects of learning (e.g. evaluating information, making conceptual links and supporting ideas with relevant evidence, etc.). Materials and assessments for the module are designed with reference to B2 and C1 descriptors of the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) and The British Association of Lecturers in English for Academic Purposes (BALEAP)’s ‘can-do’ framework for EAP syllabus design and assessment.

title: English 4
description: CDIC2020W (English 4: English for Specific Academic Purposes) is designed for Stage 2 students who are undertaking a dual undergraduate degree programme at Chang'an-Dublin International College (CDIC). The module aims to help students develop the Academic English skills that they will need in order to complete their programmes in Civil Engineering, Automotive Engineering, and Transport, City Planning and Environmental Policy. The module focuses on students’ productive skills, with a particular emphasis on writing and speaking in response to academic texts. As such, students also build on work done in Semester One on reading and summarizing discipline-specific articles, taking notes, and paraphrasing. Likewise, they further practise taking notes from lectures and summarising key points. In their writing classes, students learn how to plan, research, and produce an academic essay or report. They learn how to source and select appropriately academic articles, to critically assess what they read, and to summarize and evaluate other authors’ arguments in their own writing. They extend their understanding of citation and referencing, and of how to avoid plagiarism. This work is supported with timed writing exercises, designed to help students build confidence in writing without relying upon translation software or other aids. Students also develop their spoken production skills through short subject-specific presentations followed by question-and-answer sessions to develop their interactive skills. It is expected that autonomous student learning – particularly sourcing and reading texts – will take place outside scheduled class hours. In addition to developing language skills, classroom activities support the development of students’ academic study competences and independent language learning strategies. Students are often expected to work collaboratively in class. A particular emphasis of the module is the development of critical thinking skills. Students are encouraged to give a rationale for their decisions, to question the arguments they encounter, and to trust their own independent thinking. Classes are taught in small groups of up to 20 students. They are grouped according to the students’ specific disciplines. While many classroom tasks and activities are relevant to all academic disciplines, much of the content will be discipline-specific, and the main purpose of the module is to enable students to write and speak in English about concepts and practices within their own subject areas. Students are assessed in the following areas: continuous assessment (based on class tasks completed throughout the semester) (10%); a mid-term written assignment (an annotated bibliography) (15%), a presentation giving a critical evaluation of an academic article (15%), an end-of-semester essay of 1,500 words (35%), and two listening-into-note-taking exams (one at mid-term and one at the end of the semester)(20%). Materials and assessments for the module are designed with reference to C1 descriptors of the Common European Framework of Reference (CEFR) and The British Association of Lecturers in English for Academic Purposes (BALEAP)’s ‘can-do’ framework for EAP syllabus design and assessment.
